title: Atrophic vaginitis – Definition and overview
content: Atrophic vaginitis (genitourinary syndrome of menopause) is thinning, drying, and inflammation of the vaginal walls due to reduced oestrogen levels. It is most common in postmenopausal women but can occur at any time oestrogen levels fall, including during breastfeeding or after oophorectomy.

title: Atrophic vaginitis – Epidemiology
content: Atrophic vaginitis has an incidence of approximately 200 cases per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence is in the 50–60 year age group, corresponding to the postmenopausal period.

title: Atrophic vaginitis – Pathophysiology: oestrogen reduction
content: Reduced oestrogen levels lead to decreased vaginal blood flow, thinning of the vaginal epithelium, and loss of rugae. The vaginal pH rises from the normal acidic range (3.8–4.5) to a more alkaline environment (pH 5–7), as lactobacilli decline and the protective acidic milieu is lost.

title: Atrophic vaginitis – Clinical features: symptoms
content: Symptoms include vaginal dryness, itching, burning, and irritation; dyspareunia (painful sexual intercourse); postmenopausal vaginal bleeding or spotting; watery or yellow vaginal discharge; and urinary symptoms such as frequency, urgency, and recurrent urinary tract infections.

title: Atrophic vaginitis – Clinical features: examination findings
content: On examination, the vaginal epithelium appears pale, smooth, and dry with loss of rugae. The vaginal walls may be friable and bleed easily on contact. The labia minora may appear fused or reduced in size. A thin, watery or yellowish discharge may be present.

title: Atrophic vaginitis – Differential diagnosis
content: Key differentials include bacterial vaginosis (fishy odour, grey discharge, raised pH), vulvovaginal candidiasis (thick white discharge, intense pruritus), lichen sclerosus (white plaques, scarring), vulval dermatitis, and vulval or vaginal malignancy (especially if there is unexplained bleeding or a visible lesion).

title: Atrophic vaginitis – Management: topical oestrogens
content: First-line treatment is topical (local) oestrogen therapy, available as vaginal creams, pessaries, or rings. Topical oestrogens have minimal systemic absorption and are safe for most women, including those with a history of breast cancer when used with specialist guidance. They effectively restore vaginal epithelium, reduce pH, and relieve symptoms.

title: Atrophic vaginitis – Management: systemic HRT and other options
content: Systemic hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is appropriate when women also have systemic menopausal symptoms. Non-hormonal options include vaginal moisturisers (used regularly) and lubricants (used during intercourse). Ospemifene, a selective oestrogen receptor modulator, is an oral option for dyspareunia in women who cannot use topical oestrogens.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Definition and overview
content: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is the most common cause of abnormal vaginal discharge in women of reproductive age. It results from an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria (predominantly Gardnerella vaginalis) replacing the normal lactobacillus-dominant vaginal flora, leading to a rise in vaginal pH above 4.5.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Epidemiology
content: Bacterial vaginosis has an incidence of approximately 1,000 cases per 100,000 person-years. It is most prevalent in women aged 16–45 years. It is not classified as a sexually transmitted infection, though it is associated with sexual activity, new sexual partners, and douching.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Pathophysiology
content: Normal vaginal flora is dominated by Lactobacillus species, which maintain an acidic pH (3.8–4.5) through lactic acid production. In BV, lactobacilli are replaced by a polymicrobial overgrowth including Gardnerella vaginalis, Prevotella, Mobiluncus, and Mycoplasma hominis. This raises vaginal pH above 4.5 and produces amines (putrescine, cadaverine) responsible for the characteristic fishy odour.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Clinical features: typical presentation
content: The hallmark of BV is a thin, homogeneous, grey-white vaginal discharge with a characteristic offensive fishy odour, which is often worse after intercourse (due to alkaline semen volatilising amines). Approximately 50% of women with BV are asymptomatic. Itching and soreness are less prominent than in candidiasis.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Complications in pregnancy
content: BV in pregnancy is associated with late miscarriage, preterm labour, preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM), chorioamnionitis, and postpartum endometritis. Screening and treatment of symptomatic BV in pregnancy is recommended. BV also increases susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections including HIV, chlamydia, and gonorrhoea.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Diagnosis: Amsel's criteria
content: Diagnosis of BV requires 3 of 4 Amsel's criteria: (1) thin, homogeneous, white/grey vaginal discharge; (2) vaginal pH >4.5; (3) positive whiff test (fishy odour on adding 10% KOH to discharge); (4) clue cells on microscopy (epithelial cells studded with bacteria, obscuring cell borders). Clue cells are the most specific finding.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Differential diagnosis
content: Key differentials include: vulvovaginal candidiasis (thick white 'cottage cheese' discharge, intense pruritus, normal pH, no fishy odour); trichomoniasis (frothy yellow-green discharge, pH >4.5, strawberry cervix, STI contact); physiological discharge (clear/white, no odour, normal pH); and cervicitis due to chlamydia or gonorrhoea (mucopurulent discharge from cervical os).

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Management: symptomatic treatment
content: First-line treatment is oral metronidazole 400–500 mg twice daily for 5–7 days, or metronidazole 2 g as a single oral dose (lower cure rate). Alternative: intravaginal metronidazole gel 0.75% once daily for 5 days, or intravaginal clindamycin cream 2% once daily for 7 days. Alcohol should be avoided during metronidazole treatment and for 48 hours after.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Management in pregnancy
content: Symptomatic BV in pregnancy should be treated. Oral metronidazole is the preferred treatment (400 mg twice daily for 5–7 days). High-dose single-dose metronidazole (2 g) is not recommended in pregnancy. Intravaginal clindamycin cream should be avoided in the second half of pregnancy due to risk of neonatal adverse effects. Asymptomatic BV in low-risk pregnancies does not require routine treatment.

title: Bacterial vaginosis – Recurrent BV
content: Recurrent BV is defined as three or more episodes within 12 months. Management options include: extended courses of metronidazole (400 mg twice daily for 10–14 days), followed by maintenance therapy with intravaginal metronidazole gel twice weekly for 16 weeks. Avoidance of triggers (douching, perfumed products, new sexual partners) is advised. Boric acid vaginal suppositories may be used in recurrent cases.

title: Bartholin's cyst – Definition and overview
content: A Bartholin's cyst is a fluid-filled swelling arising from obstruction of the Bartholin's gland duct, located at the 4 and 8 o'clock positions of the vaginal introitus. When the cyst becomes infected, it forms a Bartholin's abscess, which is a common gynaecological emergency.

title: Bartholin's cyst – Epidemiology and aetiology
content: Bartholin's cysts occur in approximately 2% of women, most commonly in women of reproductive age (peak 20–30 years). Obstruction may be caused by mucus plugging, trauma, or infection. Common organisms in abscess formation include Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and sexually transmitted organisms such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis.

title: Bartholin's cyst – Clinical features
content: A Bartholin's cyst presents as a painless or mildly uncomfortable unilateral labial swelling at the vaginal introitus, typically 1–3 cm in diameter. A Bartholin's abscess presents with rapid onset of severe pain, swelling, erythema, and tenderness at the same location, often making walking and sitting difficult. Fever and systemic features may be present with abscess formation.

title: Bartholin's cyst – Management
content: Asymptomatic small cysts may be managed conservatively with observation. Symptomatic cysts or abscesses require surgical intervention. Options include: (1) Word catheter insertion (balloon catheter placed into the cyst/abscess cavity for 4–6 weeks to allow epithelialisation); (2) marsupialisation (surgical creation of a permanent opening); (3) incision and drainage (for acute abscess, though recurrence is higher). Women over 40 should have the excised tissue sent for histology to exclude Bartholin's gland carcinoma.

title: Cervical cancer – Definition and overview
content: Cervical cancer is a malignancy arising from the cervical epithelium, most commonly at the squamocolumnar junction (transformation zone). The majority (70–80%) are squamous cell carcinomas; the remainder are adenocarcinomas. It is the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide and is strongly associated with persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection.

title: Cervical cancer – Epidemiology
content: Cervical cancer has an incidence of approximately 9 cases per 100,000 person-years in the UK. Peak incidence is in women aged 30–34 years, with a second peak in women aged 60–64 years. It is the most common gynaecological cancer in women under 35 years. Incidence has declined significantly since the introduction of the national cervical screening programme.

title: Cervical cancer – Aetiology: HPV
content: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) is the primary cause of cervical cancer, responsible for over 99% of cases. HPV types 16 and 18 account for approximately 70% of cervical cancers. HPV 16 is more strongly associated with squamous cell carcinoma; HPV 18 with adenocarcinoma. HPV is transmitted sexually and most infections clear spontaneously within 1–2 years.

title: Cervical cancer – Aetiology: other risk factors
content: Additional risk factors for cervical cancer include: smoking (doubles risk; carcinogens in cervical mucus impair local immunity); immunosuppression (HIV, transplant recipients); long-term combined oral contraceptive use (>5 years, small increased risk); high number of sexual partners; early age of first sexual intercourse; lower socioeconomic status; and co-infection with other STIs (herpes simplex virus type 2, chlamydia).

title: Cervical cancer – Pathophysiology: HPV oncoproteins E6 and E7
content: High-risk HPV integrates into the host genome and produces oncoproteins E6 and E7. E6 binds to and degrades the tumour suppressor p53, preventing apoptosis. E7 binds to and inactivates the retinoblastoma protein (pRb), releasing transcription factors that drive uncontrolled cell proliferation. This leads to genomic instability and progression from cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) to invasive carcinoma.

title: Cervical cancer – Pathophysiology: CIN progression
content: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) represents a spectrum of pre-invasive changes at the transformation zone. CIN 1 (mild dysplasia) frequently regresses spontaneously. CIN 2 (moderate dysplasia) and CIN 3 (severe dysplasia/carcinoma in situ) carry higher risk of progression to invasive cancer if untreated. The average time from CIN 3 to invasive cancer is 10–15 years, allowing for effective screening intervention.

title: Cervical cancer – Clinical features
content: Early cervical cancer may be asymptomatic and detected on screening. Symptoms include: postcoital bleeding (most common presenting symptom), intermenstrual bleeding, postmenopausal bleeding, offensive or blood-stained vaginal discharge, and pelvic pain. Advanced disease may cause urinary symptoms (haematuria, frequency), rectal symptoms (rectal bleeding, altered bowel habit), and leg oedema from lymphatic obstruction.

title: Cervical cancer – FIGO staging
content: FIGO staging of cervical cancer: Stage I – confined to cervix; Stage IA – microscopic invasion (IA1: depth ≤3mm, width ≤7mm; IA2: depth 3–5mm); Stage IB – clinically visible or >5mm depth; Stage II – beyond cervix but not pelvic wall/lower third vagina; Stage IIA – no parametrial involvement; Stage IIB – parametrial involvement; Stage III – pelvic wall/lower third vagina or hydronephrosis; Stage IV – bladder/rectum (IVA) or distant metastases (IVB).

title: Cervical cancer – Management: early stage (IA–IB1)
content: Stage IA1 without lymphovascular space invasion: cone biopsy or simple hysterectomy. Stage IA1 with LVSI, IA2, and IB1: radical hysterectomy (Wertheim's hysterectomy) with pelvic lymph node dissection, or radical radiotherapy (external beam + brachytherapy). Fertility-sparing options include radical trachelectomy (removal of cervix and upper vagina, preserving uterus) for Stage IA2–IB1 with tumour <2 cm.

title: Cervical cancer – Management: locally advanced disease (IB2–IVA)
content: Locally advanced cervical cancer (Stage IB2–IVA) is treated with concurrent chemoradiotherapy: external beam radiotherapy combined with weekly cisplatin chemotherapy, followed by intracavitary brachytherapy. This is the standard of care and has superior outcomes to radiotherapy alone. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery may be considered in selected cases.

title: Cervical cancer – Complications of treatment
content: Complications of treatment include: bladder dysfunction (urinary incontinence, fistula, frequency); bowel dysfunction (diarrhoea, rectal bleeding, fistula); lymphoedema of the lower limbs; sexual dysfunction (vaginal stenosis, dyspareunia, loss of libido); premature menopause following oophorectomy or radiotherapy; and psychological morbidity. Vesicovaginal and rectovaginal fistulae are serious complications of advanced disease or radiotherapy.

title: Cervical cancer – Prognosis
content: Five-year survival rates by FIGO stage: Stage IA – >95%; Stage IB – 80–90%; Stage IIA – 70–80%; Stage IIB – 65–75%; Stage IIIA/B – 40–50%; Stage IVA – 20–30%; Stage IVB – <10%. Overall 5-year survival is approximately 63% in the UK. Prognosis is better for squamous cell carcinoma than adenocarcinoma at equivalent stages.

title: Cervical screening (HPV) – HPV-first screening programme
content: The UK cervical screening programme uses an HPV-first approach. All samples are tested for high-risk HPV (hrHPV) first. If hrHPV is negative, the sample is reported as normal and the woman is recalled at routine intervals (every 3 years aged 25–49; every 5 years aged 50–64). If hrHPV is positive, the sample undergoes cytological assessment for cell abnormalities.

title: Cervical screening (HPV) – Management of positive hrHPV with abnormal cytology
content: If hrHPV positive with abnormal cytology (borderline changes or low-grade dyskaryosis), the woman is referred for colposcopy. If hrHPV positive with high-grade dyskaryosis (moderate or severe), urgent colposcopy is arranged. At colposcopy, CIN is graded and treatment offered: CIN 1 may be observed; CIN 2 and CIN 3 are treated with large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) or laser ablation.

title: Cervical screening (HPV) – Management of positive hrHPV with negative cytology
content: If hrHPV positive but cytology is negative (no abnormal cells detected), the woman is recalled for a repeat test at 12 months. If the repeat test at 12 months is still hrHPV positive with negative cytology, she is referred for colposcopy. If hrHPV is negative at the 12-month repeat, she returns to routine recall.

title: Cervical screening (HPV) – Management of inadequate samples
content: If a cervical sample is reported as inadequate (insufficient cells for analysis), the woman should be recalled for a repeat sample after 3 months. If three consecutive samples are inadequate, she should be referred for colposcopy. Inadequate samples may result from poor sampling technique, atrophic changes, or infection.

title: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding – Definition and overview
content: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB) is abnormal uterine bleeding in the absence of recognisable pelvic pathology, general medical disease, or pregnancy. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and is most commonly caused by hormonal imbalance leading to anovulatory cycles or disturbed endometrial maturation. It accounts for the majority of cases of abnormal uterine bleeding.

title: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding – Epidemiology
content: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding is most common at the extremes of reproductive life: in adolescents (anovulatory cycles due to immature hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis) and in perimenopausal women (anovulatory cycles due to declining ovarian function). It accounts for approximately 50% of all cases of menorrhagia.

title: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding – Aetiology
content: Causes include: hormonal imbalance (anovulatory cycles, inadequate luteal phase, PCOS); structural causes (fibroids, endometrial polyps, adenomyosis, endometrial hyperplasia); systemic disease (thyroid dysfunction, coagulopathies such as von Willebrand disease, liver disease); and iatrogenic causes (anticoagulants, hormonal contraception, intrauterine devices). The FIGO PALM-COEIN classification system categorises causes as structural (PALM) and non-structural (COEIN).

title: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding – Pathophysiology
content: In anovulatory DUB, absence of progesterone following an oestrogen-stimulated proliferative phase leads to continuous endometrial proliferation without organised shedding. The endometrium becomes fragile and sheds irregularly, causing unpredictable, often heavy bleeding. In ovulatory DUB, disturbed prostaglandin balance (increased PGE2, decreased PGF2α) and impaired local haemostasis lead to excessive menstrual blood loss.

title: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding – Clinical features
content: Presentation includes irregular, unpredictable, or heavy menstrual bleeding. Perimenopausal women may have intermenstrual bleeding, prolonged periods, or amenorrhoea alternating with heavy bleeding. Features of PCOS may be present (hirsutism, obesity). Symptoms of anaemia (fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea) may develop with chronic heavy blood loss. The uterus and adnexa are typically normal on examination.

title: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding – Investigations
content: Essential investigations: pregnancy test (exclude pregnancy), full blood count (anaemia). Further investigations if indicated: TFTs (thyroid dysfunction), FSH/LH (PCOS, premature ovarian failure), prolactin (hyperprolactinaemia), androgens (PCOS). Imaging: transvaginal ultrasound (structural pathology, endometrial thickness). Endometrial biopsy (Pipelle) indicated if age >45, persistent intermenstrual bleeding, or failed treatment. Hysteroscopy and MRI if USS inconclusive.

title: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding – Management: hormonal
content: Hormonal management options: levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS/Mirena) is first-line for women not wanting pregnancy (reduces blood loss by up to 90%); combined oral contraceptive pill (regulates cycle, reduces blood loss); progestogens (norethisterone 5 mg three times daily from days 5–26 of cycle); GnRH analogues (induce temporary amenorrhoea, used short-term or pre-operatively).

title: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding – Management: non-hormonal and surgical
content: Non-hormonal options: tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic, reduces blood loss by 40–50%, taken during menstruation); NSAIDs such as mefenamic acid (reduce blood loss by 20–30%, also relieve dysmenorrhoea). Surgical options: endometrial ablation (destroys endometrium, 80% achieve amenorrhoea or light periods, not suitable if future pregnancy desired); hysterectomy (definitive treatment, reserved for failed medical/ablation therapy).

title: Ectopic pregnancy – Definition and overview
content: An ectopic pregnancy is a pregnancy in which the fertilised ovum implants outside the uterine cavity. The fallopian tube is the most common site (95–98% of cases), with the ampullary region being most frequent (70%). Other sites include the isthmus, fimbrial end, cornua, ovary, cervix, and abdominal cavity. Ectopic pregnancy is a leading cause of maternal mortality in the first trimester.

title: Ectopic pregnancy – Epidemiology
content: Ectopic pregnancy occurs in approximately 11 per 1,000 pregnancies in the UK (1.1%). Incidence has increased over recent decades, likely due to rising rates of PID, assisted reproductive technology, and improved diagnosis. It accounts for 6% of all maternal deaths. Peak incidence is in women aged 25–34 years.

title: Ectopic pregnancy – Aetiology and risk factors
content: Risk factors include: previous ectopic pregnancy (10-fold increased risk of recurrence); previous tubal surgery or sterilisation; pelvic inflammatory disease (especially Chlamydia trachomatis, which causes tubal scarring); assisted reproductive technology (IVF increases risk 2–3-fold); intrauterine contraceptive device in situ (does not prevent ectopic); endometriosis; smoking; and previous pelvic or abdominal surgery causing adhesions.

title: Ectopic pregnancy – Pathophysiology
content: Impaired tubal transport (due to ciliary dysfunction, tubal scarring, or abnormal peristalsis) prevents the fertilised ovum from reaching the uterine cavity. The embryo implants in the tube, where it cannot develop normally. As the trophoblast invades the tubal wall, it erodes blood vessels, leading to haemorrhage. Tubal rupture typically occurs at 6–10 weeks and causes life-threatening intraperitoneal haemorrhage.

title: Ectopic pregnancy – Clinical features: typical presentation
content: Classic triad: amenorrhoea (typically 6–8 weeks), lower abdominal pain (usually unilateral, colicky or sharp), and vaginal bleeding (typically dark, scanty, and less heavy than a normal period). Shoulder tip pain indicates diaphragmatic irritation from haemoperitoneum. Syncopal episodes may occur with significant haemorrhage. Pregnancy test is positive.

title: Ectopic pregnancy – Clinical features: examination findings
content: Abdominal examination may reveal unilateral tenderness, guarding, or rigidity. Pelvic examination typically shows cervical excitation (pain on moving the cervix), adnexal tenderness, and possibly an adnexal mass. In ruptured ectopic, the patient may be haemodynamically unstable (tachycardia, hypotension, pallor) with generalised peritonism. A ruptured ectopic is a surgical emergency.

title: Ectopic pregnancy – Investigations
content: Serum beta-hCG: a single level cannot confirm or exclude ectopic, but serial levels are useful (in a viable intrauterine pregnancy, hCG doubles every 48 hours; in ectopic or failing pregnancy, the rise is slower or levels fall). Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS): may show an empty uterus, adnexal mass, or free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. An intrauterine gestational sac should be visible when hCG >1,500 IU/L. Diagnostic laparoscopy is the gold standard.

title: Ectopic pregnancy – Management: expectant
content: Expectant management is appropriate for haemodynamically stable women with: serum hCG <1,000–1,500 IU/L, falling hCG levels, no fetal heartbeat on scan, no significant pain, and a reliable patient who can attend for follow-up. Serial hCG measurements are taken every 48 hours until levels fall to <20 IU/L. Approximately 50–70% of cases managed expectantly resolve without intervention.

title: Ectopic pregnancy – Management: medical (methotrexate)
content: Methotrexate (intramuscular, single dose 50 mg/m²) is used for haemodynamically stable women with: hCG <5,000 IU/L, no fetal heartbeat, ectopic mass <3.5 cm, no significant pain, and no contraindications (renal/hepatic impairment, immunodeficiency, breastfeeding). Success rate is approximately 90% when hCG <1,500 IU/L. Follow-up hCG on days 4 and 7; a second dose may be required if hCG does not fall by >15% between days 4 and 7.

title: Ectopic pregnancy – Management: surgical
content: Surgical management is indicated for haemodynamic instability, failed medical treatment, hCG >5,000 IU/L, or patient preference. Laparoscopic salpingectomy (removal of the affected tube) is the standard procedure and is preferred over salpingostomy (incision to remove ectopic, tube preserved) unless the contralateral tube is damaged. Salpingostomy carries a higher risk of persistent trophoblast (requiring methotrexate). Anti-D immunoglobulin is given to all RhD-negative women.

title: Endometrial cancer – Definition and overview
content: Endometrial cancer is the most common gynaecological malignancy in the UK, arising from the endometrial lining of the uterus. The majority (80%) are endometrioid adenocarcinomas (Type I, oestrogen-dependent, better prognosis). Type II tumours (serous, clear cell, carcinosarcoma) are less common, not oestrogen-dependent, and carry a poorer prognosis.

title: Endometrial cancer – Epidemiology
content: Endometrial cancer has an incidence of approximately 26 cases per 100,000 person-years in the UK. It is the fourth most common cancer in women. Peak incidence is in postmenopausal women aged 60–70 years; 75% of cases occur after the menopause. Incidence is rising, largely due to increasing rates of obesity.

title: Endometrial cancer – Aetiology and risk factors
content: Risk factors for Type I endometrial cancer are related to unopposed oestrogen exposure: obesity (peripheral aromatisation of androgens to oestrogen in adipose tissue), nulliparity, late menopause (>52 years), early menarche, polycystic ovarian syndrome, oestrogen-only HRT, tamoxifen use (acts as oestrogen agonist on endometrium), and diabetes mellitus. Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) carries a 40–60% lifetime risk. Protective factors include combined OCP use and multiparity.

title: Endometrial cancer – Clinical features
content: Postmenopausal bleeding is the presenting symptom in approximately 90% of cases and must be investigated urgently. In premenopausal women, presentation includes intermenstrual bleeding, menorrhagia, or irregular periods. Other features include offensive vaginal discharge (if tumour necrosis), pelvic pain (advanced disease), and systemic symptoms (weight loss, fatigue). On examination, the uterus may be enlarged.

title: Endometrial cancer – NICE referral criteria
content: NICE 2-week wait referral criteria: postmenopausal bleeding (not on HRT); postmenopausal women on HRT with unexplained bleeding after stopping HRT for 6 weeks; women aged ≥55 years with unexplained vaginal discharge who are thrombocytotic or have haematuria. Consider referral: women aged <55 years with postmenopausal bleeding; women with intermenstrual bleeding and negative examination.

title: Endometrial cancer – Investigations
content: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS): endometrial thickness >4–5 mm in postmenopausal women warrants further investigation (sensitivity 80–90% for endometrial cancer). Endometrial biopsy (Pipelle): first-line tissue sampling, performed in outpatients (sensitivity 80–90%). Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy: gold standard for visualisation and sampling. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis: staging. MRI pelvis: assesses depth of myometrial invasion and cervical involvement.

title: Endometrial cancer – FIGO 2009 staging
content: FIGO staging: Stage IA – tumour confined to endometrium or invades <50% of myometrium; Stage IB – invades ≥50% of myometrium; Stage II – cervical stromal invasion; Stage IIIA – uterine serosa or adnexa; Stage IIIB – vaginal or parametrial involvement; Stage IIIC1 – pelvic lymph node metastases; Stage IIIC2 – para-aortic lymph node metastases; Stage IVA – bladder or bowel mucosa; Stage IVB – distant metastases including inguinal nodes.

title: Endometrial cancer – Management: surgery
content: Standard surgical treatment is total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TH+BSO), performed laparoscopically where possible. Pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy is performed for staging in intermediate and high-risk disease. Omentectomy may be performed for high-grade tumours. Fertility-sparing management (progestin therapy with LNG-IUS or oral medroxyprogesterone acetate) may be considered for Stage IA, Grade 1 endometrioid cancer in young women wishing to preserve fertility.

title: Endometrial cancer – Management: adjuvant therapy
content: Adjuvant radiotherapy: vaginal brachytherapy reduces vaginal vault recurrence in intermediate-risk disease; external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) is used for high-risk or node-positive disease. Chemotherapy (paclitaxel + carboplatin) is used for advanced (Stage III–IV) or high-grade (serous, clear cell) disease. Hormonal therapy (progestogens) may be used for metastatic low-grade endometrioid cancer.

title: Endometrial cancer – Prognosis and complications
content: Five-year survival: Stage I – 85–90%; Stage II – 75%; Stage III – 45–60%; Stage IV – 15–25%. Overall 5-year survival is approximately 78%. Treatment complications include lymphoedema, bladder instability, vaginal stenosis, bowel dysfunction, vesicovaginal or rectovaginal fistulae, and premature menopause with associated osteoporosis and cardiovascular risk.

title: Endometriosis – Definition and overview
content: Endometriosis is a chronic, oestrogen-dependent inflammatory condition defined by the presence of endometrial-like tissue (glands and stroma) outside the uterine cavity. Common sites include the ovaries (endometriomas/'chocolate cysts'), pelvic peritoneum, uterosacral ligaments, rectovaginal septum, bladder, and bowel. It affects approximately 10% of women of reproductive age.

title: Endometriosis – Aetiology: theories of pathogenesis
content: Several theories explain endometriosis: (1) Retrograde menstruation (Sampson's theory) – reflux of endometrial cells through the fallopian tubes into the peritoneal cavity; (2) Coelomic metaplasia – transformation of peritoneal mesothelial cells into endometrial-like tissue; (3) Lymphatic/vascular dissemination – explains distant sites (lung, brain); (4) Genetic predisposition – first-degree relatives have a 7-fold increased risk; (5) Environmental factors – dioxin exposure may impair immune clearance of refluxed endometrial cells.

title: Endometriosis – Pathophysiology: inflammation and hormonal dysregulation
content: Ectopic endometrial tissue responds to cyclical hormonal changes, causing repeated local inflammation, cytokine release (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6), and prostaglandin production, which drives pain. Endometriotic lesions produce their own oestrogen via aromatase activity and show progesterone resistance, explaining why progestogen therapy is sometimes ineffective. Chronic inflammation leads to adhesion formation, fibrosis, and distortion of pelvic anatomy.

title: Endometriosis – Pathophysiology: subfertility mechanisms
content: Endometriosis impairs fertility through multiple mechanisms: distorted pelvic anatomy and adhesions obstructing tubal function; impaired folliculogenesis and oocyte quality; altered peritoneal fluid environment (elevated cytokines, macrophages) impairing sperm function and fertilisation; impaired endometrial receptivity reducing implantation rates; and increased risk of ectopic pregnancy. Subfertility affects approximately 30–50% of women with endometriosis.

title: Endometriosis – Clinical features
content: Classic symptoms: cyclical pelvic pain (dysmenorrhoea), chronic pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia (pain during intercourse), subfertility, and cyclical bowel or urinary symptoms (dyschezia, dysuria, haematuria, rectal bleeding) that worsen during menstruation. Symptoms do not correlate with disease stage. On examination: fixed retroverted uterus, uterosacral ligament nodularity, adnexal mass (endometrioma), and tenderness on pelvic examination. Delayed diagnosis of 4–10 years is common.

title: Endometriosis – Investigations: imaging
content: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS): first-line imaging; can identify ovarian endometriomas (chocolate cysts with ground-glass echogenicity) and deep infiltrating endometriosis of the rectovaginal septum and bladder. Pelvic MRI: superior to USS for mapping deep infiltrating endometriosis, particularly bowel and bladder involvement, and for surgical planning. A normal ultrasound does not exclude endometriosis.

title: Endometriosis – Investigations: diagnostic laparoscopy and CA125
content: Diagnostic laparoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis. It allows direct visualisation and biopsy of lesions, and surgical removal at the same procedure. Findings include: fixed retroverted uterus, endometriomas, chocolate cysts, adhesions, peritoneal deposits, and powder-burn lesions. Serum CA125 is not used to diagnose endometriosis; a raised level (>35 IU/ml) may be consistent with endometriosis but is non-specific.

title: Endometriosis – Differential diagnosis
content: Key differentials: primary dysmenorrhoea (pelvic pain, no pelvic findings); adenomyosis (enlarged boggy uterus, endometrial tissue in myometrium on MRI); PID (fever, abnormal discharge, positive STI swabs); ovarian cyst (simple follicular cyst, not endometrioma); PCOS (irregular periods, multiple simple cysts, no other pelvic deposits); IBS/IBD (GI symptoms, no cyclical pattern, positive GI investigations); interstitial cystitis (urinary symptoms, negative imaging, positive dipstick).

title: Endometriosis – ASRM staging
content: The ASRM (American Society for Reproductive Medicine) classification stages endometriosis based on laparoscopic findings: Stage I (minimal) – isolated implants, no adhesions; Stage II (mild) – superficial implants <5 cm, no adhesions; Stage III (moderate) – multiple superficial and deep implants, peritubal/periovarian adhesions; Stage IV (severe) – multiple deep implants, large endometriomas, dense adhesions. Limitations: stage does not correlate with symptom severity; patients with Stage I may have severe pain.

title: Endometriosis – Management: analgesia (NICE 2017)
content: A short trial (3 months) of paracetamol or an NSAID alone or in combination is recommended as first-line management for endometriosis-related pain. If pain relief is inadequate, consider hormonal treatments or referral to secondary care. NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated pain and are effective for dysmenorrhoea. Opioids may be required for severe pain but are not recommended for long-term use.

title: Endometriosis – Management: hormonal treatment
content: Hormonal treatments suppress ovarian function and oestrogen production, reducing lesion activity and pain. Options include: combined oral contraceptive pill (oestrogen + progesterone); progestogen-only contraceptives (pill, implant, IUS, injection); GnRH agonists (induce temporary menopause, used short-term due to bone density loss; add-back HRT may be used); GnRH antagonists; androgenic agents (danazol – rarely used due to side effects). All hormonal treatments act as contraceptives and should be discussed with the patient.

title: Endometriosis – Management: surgical treatment
content: Surgical treatment via laparoscopy is the only potentially curative option. It involves systematic inspection of the pelvis, biopsy of suspected lesions, and removal or ablation of endometriotic deposits. Laparoscopic excision is preferred over ablation for deep infiltrating disease. Endometriomas should be excised (cystectomy) rather than drained. Hysterectomy with BSO may be considered for severe, refractory disease in women who have completed their family. Surgery improves pain and fertility outcomes.

title: Fibroid degeneration – Definition and overview
content: Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) are common benign tumours of smooth muscle affecting approximately 20% of women of reproductive age. 'Red' (carneous) degeneration describes ischaemic necrosis of myocytes secondary to outgrowing their blood supply and is the most common form of fibroid degeneration. It most commonly presents during pregnancy when increased circulating oestrogen drives rapid fibroid growth.

title: Fibroid degeneration – Epidemiology and aetiology
content: Fibroid degeneration complicates approximately 5% of pregnancies complicated by fibroids. Risk factors for fibroids include: African-Caribbean ethnicity (3–9 times higher incidence), age 30–50 years, nulliparity, obesity, and family history. Fibroids are oestrogen-dependent and regress after the menopause. Red degeneration is most common in the second trimester (12th–22nd week) of pregnancy.

title: Fibroid degeneration – Pathophysiology
content: During pregnancy, rising oestrogen and progesterone levels stimulate rapid fibroid growth. When the fibroid outgrows its blood supply, central ischaemia leads to haemorrhagic infarction of myocytes (red/carneous degeneration). The fibroid becomes oedematous and haemorrhagic, with a characteristic red appearance on cut section. This triggers an acute inflammatory response causing localised peritonism.

title: Fibroid degeneration – Clinical features
content: Typical presentation is in the second trimester of pregnancy (12th–22nd week) with acute localised abdominal pain over the fibroid, low-grade fever (37.5–38.5°C), and uterine tenderness. The pain may be severe and constant. Nausea and vomiting may occur. Vital signs show mild tachycardia. Fetal heart rate is typically normal. The uterus is tender on palpation, often with localised peritonism over the fibroid.

title: Fibroid degeneration – Investigations
content: Blood tests: full blood count (raised white cell count, elevated CRP indicating inflammation), but these are non-specific. Ultrasound: confirms fibroid location and size; may show heterogeneous echogenicity within the fibroid consistent with degeneration. MRI: more sensitive for detecting degeneration (shows characteristic signal changes). CTG: continuous fetal monitoring to assess fetal wellbeing. Urine culture: to exclude urinary tract infection as a differential.

title: Fibroid degeneration – Management
content: Management during pregnancy is conservative: reassurance, adequate analgesia (paracetamol first-line; opioids such as codeine or morphine for severe pain), hydration, and rest. NSAIDs should be used with caution in pregnancy due to risk of premature closure of the ductus arteriosus (avoid after 28 weeks). Surgical myomectomy during pregnancy is rarely indicated due to high risk of haemorrhage and preterm labour. Symptoms typically resolve within 1–2 weeks.

title: Gestational trophoblastic disorders – Definition and classification
content: Gestational trophoblastic disorders (GTD) are a spectrum of conditions arising from abnormal proliferation of placental trophoblastic tissue. They include: complete hydatidiform mole (benign, all chromosomes paternal); partial hydatidiform mole (benign, triploid); invasive mole; choriocarcinoma (malignant); and placental site trophoblastic tumour. Collectively, gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) refers to the malignant forms requiring chemotherapy.

title: Gestational trophoblastic disorders – Complete hydatidiform mole: genetics and pathology
content: A complete hydatidiform mole occurs when an empty (anucleate) egg is fertilised by a single sperm that then duplicates its own DNA, resulting in a diploid karyotype (46XX or 46XY) in which all chromosomes are of paternal origin (androgenetic). No fetal parts are present. The trophoblast proliferates abnormally, producing grape-like vesicles. Approximately 2–3% progress to choriocarcinoma.

title: Gestational trophoblastic disorders – Complete mole: clinical features
content: Clinical features of a complete hydatidiform mole: vaginal bleeding in the first or early second trimester; exaggerated symptoms of pregnancy (severe hyperemesis); uterus large for dates; very high serum hCG levels (often >100,000 IU/L); hypertension (pre-eclampsia before 20 weeks); hyperthyroidism (hCG mimics TSH). On ultrasound: 'snowstorm' appearance with no fetal parts.

title: Gestational trophoblastic disorders – Complete mole: management
content: Management: urgent referral to a specialist trophoblastic disease centre; suction curettage (evacuation of the uterus) under ultrasound guidance; histological examination of evacuated material. Effective contraception is recommended to avoid pregnancy for the next 12 months (to allow hCG monitoring). Serial serum hCG measurements are performed to detect persistent GTD or malignant transformation. Anti-D immunoglobulin is given to RhD-negative women.

title: Gestational trophoblastic disorders – Partial hydatidiform mole
content: A partial hydatidiform mole occurs when a normal haploid egg is fertilised by two sperms, or by one sperm with duplication of paternal chromosomes, resulting in a triploid karyotype (69XXX, 69XXY, or 69XYY). Both maternal and paternal chromosomes are present. Fetal parts may be seen on ultrasound. Clinical features are less dramatic than a complete mole; hCG levels are lower. Risk of malignant transformation is approximately 0.5–1%.

title: Miscarriage – Definition and epidemiology
content: Miscarriage is defined as the spontaneous loss of pregnancy before 24 weeks of gestation. It occurs in approximately 30% of all pregnancies (including unrecognised pregnancies) and in 1 in 8 known pregnancies. Most miscarriages occur in the first trimester. Incidence is approximately 350 cases per 100,000 person-years, with peak incidence at age 30–40 years. Recurrent miscarriage (3 or more consecutive losses) affects approximately 1% of couples.

title: Miscarriage – Aetiology: fetal and maternal causes
content: Chromosomal abnormalities are the most common cause of first trimester miscarriage (50–60% of cases). Other causes: antiphospholipid syndrome (present in 15% of women with recurrent miscarriage, particularly first trimester); thrombophilia (factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation – associated with second trimester loss); endocrine disorders (PCOS, thyroid disease, diabetes, hyperprolactinaemia); infections (bacterial vaginosis associated with late miscarriage); uterine abnormalities (septate, bicornuate, or arcuate uterus; cervical incompetence; fibroids).

title: Miscarriage – Aetiology: risk factors for further miscarriage
content: The two most important risk factors for further miscarriage are increasing maternal age (93% risk of miscarriage in women aged ≥45 years) and previous miscarriages (40% risk of further miscarriage after three consecutive losses). Other risk factors include: smoking, obesity, stress, high-dose radiation, heavy metal exposure, sperm abnormalities, old paternal age, and tight clothing in males.

title: Miscarriage – Classification of types
content: Miscarriage types: Complete – all products of conception expelled, bleeding stops, no further treatment needed. Incomplete – fetus expelled but placenta partially retained, bleeding persists, surgical management often needed. Missed (silent) – fetus died in utero, no symptoms, small for dates uterus, diagnosed on ultrasound. Threatened – viable pregnancy with bleeding and closed cervical os; 75% settle. Inevitable – non-viable pregnancy with bleeding and open cervical os. Recurrent – 3 or more consecutive miscarriages (1% of patients).

title: Miscarriage – Clinical features
content: Clinical features vary by type. Common features: vaginal bleeding (ranging from brownish spotting to heavy bright-red blood with clots, occurring in 20–30% of pregnant women in the first trimester); lower abdominal cramping pain; vaginal fluid or tissue discharge; loss of pregnancy symptoms (nausea, breast tenderness); lower back pain. A missed miscarriage often presents with no symptoms and is diagnosed incidentally on ultrasound.

title: Miscarriage – Referral criteria
content: Immediate hospital admission: any haemodynamic instability. Immediate referral to EPAU or out-of-hours gynaecology: suspicion of ectopic pregnancy. Referral to EPAU: symptoms suggesting early pregnancy problem (excluding abdominal pain, pelvic tenderness, cervical motion tenderness) and >6 weeks pregnant or unknown gestation; any doubt about pregnancy viability. If bleeding but no pain and <6 weeks pregnant: expectant management with repeat pregnancy test after 7–10 days.

title: Miscarriage – Investigations
content: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS): confirms location and viability of pregnancy; if status unclear, repeat scan after minimum 7 days. Serum beta-hCG: serial measurements to assess trend (falling levels confirm miscarriage; rising levels suggest viable pregnancy or ectopic). Recurrent miscarriage investigations: karyotyping of both partners; TVUS for structural abnormalities; antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant); thrombophilia screen.

title: Miscarriage – Management: expectant, medical, and surgical
content: Expectant management (first-line, NICE 2023): wait 7–14 days for spontaneous completion; suitable for haemodynamically stable women. Medical management: mifepristone 200 mg orally followed 24–48 hours later by misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally (for missed miscarriage); misoprostol alone for incomplete miscarriage. Surgical management: vacuum aspiration (manual or electric) under local or general anaesthesia; surgical management preferred if haemodynamic instability, infection, or failed medical management.

title: Miscarriage – Complications
content: Complications include: incomplete miscarriage with retained products of conception requiring surgical evacuation; haemorrhagic shock (especially with incomplete or inevitable miscarriage); infection/sepsis (endometritis, approximately 3% of cases); psychological morbidity (grief, depression, anxiety, PTSD); Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions) following repeated surgical evacuation; and sensitisation in RhD-negative women (anti-D immunoglobulin required for all surgical and some medical management).

title: Ovarian torsion – Definition and overview
content: Ovarian torsion is the twisting of the ovary (and often the fallopian tube) on its pedicle, causing obstruction of venous drainage followed by arterial occlusion, leading to ischaemia and potential necrosis. It is an acute gynaecological emergency requiring prompt surgical intervention to preserve ovarian function. It accounts for approximately 3% of gynaecological emergencies.

title: Ovarian torsion – Epidemiology
content: Ovarian torsion has an incidence of approximately 6 cases per 100,000 person-years. It predominantly affects women of reproductive age (peak 20–30 years) but can occur at any age including in children and postmenopausal women. It is more common on the right side (due to the sigmoid colon limiting left-sided torsion). It is the fifth most common gynaecological emergency.

title: Ovarian torsion – Aetiology and risk factors
content: Risk factors: ovarian masses >5 cm (most important – benign cysts, dermoid cysts, endometriomas increase risk); reproductive age (hormonal influences increase ovarian size); pregnancy (corpus luteum cysts, increased ovarian mobility); ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (from fertility treatment); previous ovarian surgery; and abnormally long utero-ovarian ligaments (congenital). In children, torsion may occur on a normal ovary.

title: Ovarian torsion – Pathophysiology
content: Torsion initially obstructs venous and lymphatic drainage, causing ovarian oedema and enlargement. Progressive twisting then occludes arterial supply, leading to ischaemia and infarction. Inflammatory mediators (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6) are released, causing peritoneal irritation and pain. Reperfusion injury (reactive oxygen species) may occur if detorsion is performed after prolonged ischaemia. Necrosis and loss of ovarian function occur if untreated.

title: Ovarian torsion – Clinical features
content: Classic presentation: sudden onset, severe, unilateral pelvic pain (often colicky, radiating to the groin, flank, or back), nausea and vomiting (in up to 70%), and low-grade fever if necrosis is present. Pain may be intermittent (intermittent torsion with spontaneous detorsion). On examination: unilateral adnexal tenderness, possible adnexal mass, and peritoneal signs if necrosis. Haemodynamic instability is rare unless rupture occurs.

title: Ovarian torsion – Investigations
content: Pregnancy test: mandatory first step to exclude ectopic pregnancy. Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler: first-line imaging; may show enlarged ovary, peripherally displaced follicles, free pelvic fluid, and absent or reduced blood flow. Normal Doppler does not exclude torsion (intermittent torsion). MRI: useful when ultrasound inconclusive; high-resolution imaging differentiates adnexal masses. Laparoscopy: gold standard for diagnosis and immediate treatment; negative imaging should not delay surgery if clinical suspicion is high.

title: Ovarian torsion – Differential diagnosis
content: Key differentials: ectopic pregnancy (unilateral pain, positive hCG, absent intrauterine sac on USS); appendicitis (pain migrating from periumbilical to right iliac fossa, fever, raised WCC, no adnexal mass); pelvic inflammatory disease (bilateral pain, abnormal discharge, cervical excitation, positive STI swabs); ruptured ovarian cyst (sudden pain, free fluid on USS, often less severe); urolithiasis (loin to groin pain, haematuria, no adnexal mass).

title: Ovarian torsion – Management
content: Initial management: IV fluids, analgesia, and urgent pelvic ultrasound. Surgical intervention: laparoscopy should be performed irrespective of ultrasound findings if clinical suspicion is high. Conservative management via detorsion (untwisting the ovary) is attempted first, even if the ovary appears ischaemic (black/blue), as recovery is possible. Oophorectomy is only performed if necrosis is confirmed or detorsion fails. Follow-up ultrasound at 6 weeks post-operatively to assess ovarian function.

title: Placenta praevia – Definition and classification
content: Placenta praevia occurs when the placenta implants in the lower uterine segment, partially or completely covering the internal cervical os. AIUM/RCOG classification: Grade 1 (low-lying) – lower edge 0.5–2 cm from internal os; Grade 2 (marginal) – reaches but does not cover the os; Grade 3 (partial) – partially covers the os; Grade 4 (complete) – completely covers the os. Prognosis worsens with higher grades.

title: Placenta praevia – Epidemiology
content: Placenta praevia has an incidence of approximately 20 cases per 100,000 person-years. Low-lying placenta is found in 4–6% of pregnancies before 20 weeks; however, up to 90% of these resolve spontaneously as the uterus grows (placental migration). Only 10% of complete praevias resolve. Incidence is rising due to increasing caesarean section rates.

title: Placenta praevia – Aetiology and risk factors
content: Risk factors: previous uterine scarring (most important – caesarean section, uterine rupture, endometriosis, D&C); previous placenta praevia (increases risk to 4–8% in subsequent pregnancies); multiparity and multiple pregnancies; advanced maternal age; smoking; and assisted reproductive technology. The mechanism involves abnormal trophoblastic invasion of the lower uterine segment, possibly due to scarring directing implantation inferiorly.

title: Placenta praevia – Clinical features
content: The hallmark is painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding, typically after 20 weeks (mean gestational age at first bleed: 30 weeks; one-third present before this). Severity ranges from spotting to life-threatening haemorrhage. The uterus is not tender (unlike placental abruption). Fetal presentation may be abnormal (transverse or oblique lie, unstable lie). Vaginal and rectal examinations are contraindicated. Intercourse should be avoided.

title: Placenta praevia – Investigations
content: Transabdominal ultrasound detects placenta praevia in approximately 95% of cases; transvaginal ultrasound in nearly 100%. Typically detected at 20-week anomaly scan. Follow-up transvaginal USS at 32 weeks for persistent low-lying placenta; if still present, repeat at 36 weeks to plan delivery. Additional investigations: FBC (anaemia, platelet disorder), clotting studies (if platelets abnormal), blood type and cross-match, Kleihauer test (RhD-negative mothers), CTG (fetal wellbeing), LFTs and U&E (exclude pre-eclampsia).

title: Placenta praevia – Differential diagnosis
content: Key differentials for antepartum haemorrhage: placental abruption (painful, tender uterus, concealed or revealed bleeding, fetal compromise); miscarriage (cramping pain, products of conception, more common in first/second trimester); placenta accreta (abnormally invasive placenta, associated with uterine scarring, diagnosed on USS/MRI); local causes (cervical ectropion, cervical polyps, cervicitis, genital lacerations, malignancy).

title: Placenta praevia – Management
content: Acute haemorrhage: ABCDE approach, IV access, FBC/cross-match, corticosteroids if <34 weeks, tocolytics if contracting, anti-D if RhD-negative, caesarean section if maternal/fetal compromise. Routine management: pelvic rest (no intercourse, no vaginal examination), corticosteroids at 34–36 weeks, follow-up USS. Delivery planning: Grade 1/2 may attempt vaginal delivery if lower edge >2 cm from os; Grade 3/4 (major praevia) require elective caesarean at 37–38 weeks.

title: Placenta praevia – Complications
content: Maternal complications: major haemorrhage requiring blood transfusion; emergency caesarean section; hysterectomy (if placenta accreta co-exists or haemorrhage uncontrollable); maternal death. Fetal complications: preterm birth (most common); intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR); fetal death from haemorrhage or hypoxia; malpresentation requiring caesarean. Placenta accreta spectrum (accreta, increta, percreta) is a serious complication associated with previous uterine scarring.

title: Placental abruption – Definition and overview
content: Placental abruption is the premature separation of a normally sited placenta from the uterine wall before delivery of the fetus. It is a major cause of antepartum haemorrhage (accounting for approximately 30% of cases) and a significant cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. Bleeding may be revealed (external), concealed (behind the placenta), or mixed.

title: Placental abruption – Aetiology and risk factors
content: Risk factors: pre-eclampsia and hypertension (most important); smoking; cocaine use; abdominal trauma; chorioamnionitis; alcohol use; advanced maternal age; multiparity; previous placental abruption (recurrence risk approximately 8% in subsequent pregnancy, rising to 25% after two abruptions); thrombophilia; premature rupture of membranes; and polyhydramnios (sudden uterine decompression).

title: Placental abruption – Clinical features
content: Vaginal bleeding (variable volume; 20% of abruptions are concealed with no external bleeding); sudden onset severe abdominal pain (constant, not colicky); uterine tenderness and rigidity ('woody' uterus); uterine hypertonicity; fetal compromise (abnormal CTG, fetal bradycardia); and maternal shock (disproportionate to visible blood loss if concealed). Back pain may be present. Fetal parts may be difficult to palpate due to uterine rigidity.

title: Placental abruption – Investigations
content: Ultrasound: may show retroplacental haematoma (sensitivity only 25–50%; a normal scan does not exclude abruption). CTG: essential for fetal wellbeing assessment. Blood tests: FBC (anaemia, thrombocytopaenia), coagulation profile (DIC – prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer), Kleihauer-Betke test (quantify feto-maternal haemorrhage in RhD-negative women), LFTs and renal function (exclude pre-eclampsia), cross-match.

title: Placental abruption – Management
content: Initial resuscitation: ABCDE, IV access (2 large-bore cannulae), blood transfusion, FFP/cryoprecipitate for DIC. Delivery: immediate delivery if maternal or fetal compromise (emergency caesarean section); conservative management if <37 weeks without compromise (aim for vaginal delivery if possible). Corticosteroids: single dose between 24th and 34th weeks (preterm birth risk). Anti-D immunoglobulin: all non-sensitised RhD-negative women regardless of prior prophylaxis. Active management of third stage of labour to prevent PPH.

title: Placental abruption – Complications
content: Maternal complications: severe haemorrhage and hypovolaemic shock; disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC); acute kidney injury; hysterectomy (to control bleeding); maternal death; recurrence in future pregnancies. Fetal complications: premature birth; stillbirth; low birth weight; hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy; cerebral palsy. Couvelaire uterus (extravasation of blood into myometrium) may impair uterine contractility and worsen PPH.

title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Definition and overview
content: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a complex endocrine disorder affecting 5–20% of women of reproductive age. It is characterised by a combination of ovarian dysfunction, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound. The aetiology involves both hyperinsulinaemia and elevated luteinising hormone, with overlap with the metabolic syndrome.

title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Epidemiology
content: PCOS has an incidence of approximately 90 cases per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence is in women aged 30–40 years. It is the most common endocrine disorder in women of reproductive age and the most common cause of anovulatory infertility.

title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Clinical features
content: Clinical features: subfertility and infertility (anovulatory cycles); menstrual disturbances (oligomenorrhoea, amenorrhoea); hirsutism and acne (due to hyperandrogenism); obesity (present in 50–80%); acanthosis nigricans (due to insulin resistance); and psychological symptoms (depression, anxiety). Women with PCOS are at increased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, endometrial cancer, and obstructive sleep apnoea.

title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Investigations
content: Pelvic ultrasound: polycystic ovaries defined as ≥12 follicles (2–9 mm diameter) in one or both ovaries and/or increased ovarian volume (>10 cm³). Hormonal profile: FSH, LH (raised LH:FSH ratio is classical but no longer required for diagnosis), prolactin (may be mildly elevated), TSH (exclude thyroid disease), testosterone (may be mildly elevated; if markedly raised, consider other causes such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia or androgen-secreting tumour). Glucose tolerance test: screen for impaired glucose tolerance/type 2 diabetes.

title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Diagnosis: Rotterdam criteria
content: The Rotterdam criteria (most widely used) require 2 of the following 3 features: (1) oligo- and/or anovulation (oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea); (2) clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, or elevated total/free testosterone); (3) polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (≥12 follicles 2–9 mm in one or both ovaries and/or ovarian volume >10 cm³). Other causes of hyperandrogenism must be excluded.

title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Management: general and hirsutism
content: General: weight reduction (even 5–10% weight loss can restore ovulation and improve metabolic parameters); combined oral contraceptive pill (regulates cycle, induces monthly bleed, reduces androgen levels). Hirsutism and acne: third-generation COCP (fewer androgenic effects) or co-cyprindiol (anti-androgen action; increased VTE risk). If COCP fails: topical eflornithine; spironolactone, flutamide, or finasteride under specialist supervision.

title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Management: infertility
content: Infertility management in PCOS should be supervised by a specialist. Weight reduction is first-line. Clomifene (anti-oestrogen, blocks hypothalamic oestrogen receptors, stimulates FSH secretion) is the most effective treatment for ovulation induction (2007 NEJM trial). Risk of multiple pregnancy with clomifene. Metformin (alone or combined with clomifene) is used particularly in obese patients; RCOG (2008) concluded metformin is not first-line. Gonadotrophins and laparoscopic ovarian drilling are second-line options.

title: Premature ovarian failure – Definition, epidemiology, and aetiology
content: Premature ovarian failure (POF), also called premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), is cessation of normal ovarian function before the age of 40 years. Incidence is approximately 30 cases per 100,000 person-years; affects approximately 1% of women under 40 and 0.1% under 30. Causes include: genetic disorders (Turner syndrome, fragile X premutation); autoimmune disease (most common cause in developed countries); iatrogenic (chemotherapy, pelvic radiotherapy, bilateral oophorectomy); and idiopathic (50% of cases).

title: Premature ovarian failure – Clinical features and management
content: Clinical features: secondary amenorrhoea (primary presenting symptom); climacteric symptoms (hot flushes, night sweats, vaginal dryness); infertility; and features of the underlying cause. Investigations: raised FSH (>25 IU/L on two occasions ≥4 weeks apart), low oestradiol, low AMH. Management: hormone replacement therapy (HRT) until the natural age of menopause (51 years) to prevent osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease; fertility treatment (oocyte donation is most effective); psychological support.

title: Premenstrual syndrome – Definition and overview
content: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) describes the emotional and physical symptoms experienced during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle that resolve with the onset of menstruation. It only occurs in the presence of ovulatory menstrual cycles and does not occur prior to puberty, during pregnancy, or after the menopause. Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a severe form meeting DSM-5 criteria.

title: Premenstrual syndrome – Epidemiology
content: PMS has an incidence of approximately 500 cases per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence is in women aged 30–40 years. Up to 80% of women experience some premenstrual symptoms; approximately 5–8% have severe symptoms meeting criteria for PMDD. PMS is the most common gynaecological complaint in women of reproductive age.

title: Premenstrual syndrome – Clinical features
content: Emotional/psychological features: mood swings, irritability, increased anger, anxiety, tension, low mood, tearfulness, difficulty concentrating. Physical features: breast tenderness or swelling, bloating and abdominal discomfort, headache, fatigue, increased appetite (carbohydrate cravings), sleep disturbance. Symptoms occur exclusively in the luteal phase (after ovulation) and remit shortly after menstruation begins. Symptom-free intervals during the follicular phase are essential for diagnosis.

title: Premenstrual syndrome – Management
content: Mild PMS: lifestyle advice (regular exercise, dietary modification, stress reduction, sleep hygiene). Moderate PMS: new-generation combined oral contraceptive pill containing drospirenone 3 mg + ethinylestradiol 0.030 mg (e.g., Yasmin) – drospirenone has anti-mineralocorticoid and anti-androgenic properties. Severe PMS/PMDD: SSRIs (e.g., fluoxetine, sertraline) given continuously or in the luteal phase only (days 15–28 of cycle) – effective for emotional symptoms.

title: Ruptured ovarian cysts – Definition and overview
content: Ovarian cyst rupture occurs when the wall of an ovarian cyst breaks, releasing its contents into the peritoneal cavity. It is a common cause of acute pelvic pain in women of reproductive age. Most ruptured cysts are benign functional cysts (follicular or corpus luteum cysts). Haemorrhagic cysts may cause significant haemoperitoneum requiring surgical intervention.

title: Ruptured ovarian cysts – Aetiology and clinical features
content: Aetiology: spontaneous rupture (most common), physical activity, trauma, sexual intercourse, or increased intra-abdominal pressure. Clinical features: sudden onset, unilateral, sharp pelvic pain (may become diffuse if haemoperitoneum); nausea and vomiting; peritoneal signs (guarding, rebound tenderness) if haemoperitoneum; haemodynamic instability if significant haemorrhage; low-grade fever; and urinary or GI symptoms. On examination: unilateral adnexal tenderness, possible cervical excitation.

title: Ruptured ovarian cysts – Differential diagnosis
content: Key differentials: ectopic pregnancy (positive hCG, absent intrauterine sac on USS, cervical excitation); ovarian torsion (severe colicky pain, enlarged ovary, absent Doppler flow); appendicitis (right iliac fossa pain, fever, raised WCC, no adnexal mass); PID (bilateral pain, discharge, positive STI swabs, fever); urolithiasis (loin to groin pain, haematuria, no adnexal mass); diverticulitis (left iliac fossa pain, fever, altered bowel habit).

title: Ruptured ovarian cysts – Management
content: Conservative management for haemodynamically stable patients: analgesia (NSAIDs, paracetamol, opioids), IV fluids, serial observations, and serial haematocrit monitoring. Surgical management (laparoscopic preferred): indicated for haemodynamic instability, significant haemoperitoneum, ongoing haemorrhage, or diagnostic uncertainty. Laparotomy may be required for massive haemorrhage. Ovarian cystectomy (preserving ovary) is preferred over oophorectomy. Histology of excised tissue is recommended.

title: Urogenital prolapse – Definition and types
content: Urogenital (pelvic organ) prolapse is the descent of one or more pelvic organs (bladder, uterus, vaginal vault, rectum) into or beyond the vaginal canal due to weakness of the pelvic floor support structures. Types: anterior compartment (cystocele – bladder prolapse; urethrocele – urethral prolapse); posterior compartment (rectocele – rectal prolapse; enterocele – small bowel prolapse); apical compartment (uterine prolapse; vault prolapse post-hysterectomy).

title: Urogenital prolapse – Epidemiology and aetiology
content: Pelvic organ prolapse affects approximately 50% of parous women to some degree; symptomatic prolapse affects 10–20%. Peak incidence is in women aged 70+. Risk factors: vaginal childbirth (most important – especially prolonged second stage, instrumental delivery, large baby); multiparity; obesity; chronic increased intra-abdominal pressure (constipation, chronic cough, heavy lifting); oestrogen deficiency (postmenopause); connective tissue disorders; and previous pelvic surgery.

title: Urogenital prolapse – Pathophysiology
content: Normal pelvic floor support depends on the levator ani muscle complex (pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus, puborectalis) and the endopelvic fascia (pubocervical fascia anteriorly, rectovaginal fascia posteriorly, cardinal and uterosacral ligaments apically). Childbirth causes direct muscle trauma, pudendal nerve injury, and fascial tears. Oestrogen deficiency leads to atrophy of supporting tissues. Chronic increased intra-abdominal pressure progressively weakens these structures.

title: Urogenital prolapse – Clinical features
content: Symptoms: sensation of a vaginal bulge or 'something coming down' (most common complaint); urinary symptoms (stress incontinence, urgency, frequency, incomplete bladder emptying, recurrent UTIs); defecatory dysfunction (constipation, incomplete evacuation, need to digitally reduce prolapse to defaecate); sexual dysfunction (dyspareunia, reduced sensation); and low back or pelvic pressure. Symptoms worsen with prolonged standing and improve with lying down.

title: Urogenital prolapse – Management: conservative
content: Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) is first-line for Stage I–II prolapse; supervised PFMT for at least 3–6 months before considering surgery. Vaginal pessaries (ring, shelf, or Gellhorn pessaries) provide mechanical support and are suitable for women who decline surgery, are unfit for surgery, or during pregnancy. Topical oestrogen improves vaginal tissue quality and reduces pessary complications. Lifestyle modifications: weight loss, treat constipation, avoid heavy lifting.

title: Urogenital prolapse – Management: surgical
content: Surgical options: anterior colporrhaphy (repair of cystocele); posterior colporrhaphy (repair of rectocele); sacrocolpopexy (abdominal/laparoscopic fixation of vaginal vault to sacrum using mesh – gold standard for vault prolapse); sacrospinous fixation (vaginal approach, fixes vault to sacrospinous ligament); Manchester repair (amputation of cervix + anterior repair); hysterectomy (if uterine prolapse). Mesh use in vaginal prolapse surgery is restricted in the UK due to complications (pain, erosion, dyspareunia).

title: Vaginal candidiasis – Definition, epidemiology, and aetiology
content: Vaginal candidiasis (vulvovaginal candidiasis) is a fungal infection of the vagina and vulva, caused by Candida species in 80–90% of cases by Candida albicans. It is the second most common cause of vaginal discharge after bacterial vaginosis. Incidence is approximately 200 cases per 100,000 person-years; peak age 25–35 years. Risk factors: diabetes mellitus, antibiotic use (disrupts normal flora), corticosteroids, pregnancy, immunosuppression (HIV), and tight synthetic clothing.

title: Vaginal candidiasis – Clinical features
content: Symptoms: intense vulval pruritus (most prominent symptom), vulval soreness and burning, thick white 'cottage cheese' or curd-like vaginal discharge (typically odourless), dyspareunia, and external dysuria (burning on micturition). Signs: vulval and vaginal erythema and oedema, adherent white plaques on vaginal walls, excoriation, and fissuring. The absence of offensive odour and the presence of marked erythema help distinguish candidiasis from BV.

title: Vaginal candidiasis – Management: acute and recurrent
content: Acute treatment: local (intravaginal) clotrimazole 500 mg pessary as a single dose (first-line); oral fluconazole 150 mg as a single dose (equally effective, preferred by many women); oral itraconazole 200 mg twice daily for 1 day as alternative. In pregnancy: local treatments only (clotrimazole); oral azoles are contraindicated. Recurrent candidiasis (≥4 episodes per year, BASHH definition): induction with fluconazole 150 mg every 3 days for 3 doses, followed by maintenance fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months.

title: Combined contraceptive patch – Mechanism and cycle
content: The Evra patch is the only combined contraceptive patch licensed for use in the UK. The patch cycle lasts 4 weeks: the patch is worn and changed weekly for 3 consecutive weeks, followed by a patch-free week during which a withdrawal bleed occurs.

title: Combined contraceptive patch – Delayed patch change at end of week 1 or 2
content: If the patch change is delayed at the end of week 1 or week 2: if the delay is less than 48 hours, change immediately and no further precautions are needed. If the delay is greater than 48 hours, change immediately and use barrier contraception for the next 7 days. If unprotected sex occurred during the extended patch-free interval or in the last 5 days, emergency contraception must be considered.

title: Combined contraceptive patch – Delayed patch removal at end of week 3
content: If patch removal is delayed at the end of week 3, remove the patch as soon as possible and apply the new patch on the usual cycle start day for the next cycle, even if withdrawal bleeding is occurring. No additional contraception is needed.

title: Combined contraceptive patch – Delayed application at start of new cycle
content: If patch application is delayed at the end of a patch-free week (i.e., delayed start of a new cycle), additional barrier contraception should be used for 7 days following any delay at the start of a new patch cycle.

title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Advantages
content: Advantages of the COCP: highly effective (failure rate <1 per 100 woman-years); does not interfere with sex; reversible on stopping; usually makes periods regular, lighter, and less painful; reduced risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer (effect may last several decades after cessation); reduced risk of colorectal cancer; may protect against pelvic inflammatory disease; may reduce ovarian cysts, benign breast disease, and acne vulgaris.

title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Disadvantages
content: Disadvantages of the COCP: requires daily adherence; offers no protection against sexually transmitted infections; increased risk of venous thromboembolic disease; increased risk of breast and cervical cancer; increased risk of stroke and ischaemic heart disease (especially in smokers); temporary side-effects including headache, nausea, and breast tenderness. A Cochrane review did not support a causal relationship between COCP use and weight gain.

title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – UKMEC contraindications: UKMEC 3 conditions
content: UKMEC 3 conditions for the COCP (disadvantages generally outweigh advantages): age >35 years and smoking <15 cigarettes/day; BMI >35 kg/m²; family history of thromboembolic disease in first-degree relatives aged <45 years; controlled hypertension; immobility (e.g. wheelchair use); carrier of known gene mutations associated with breast cancer (e.g. BRCA1/BRCA2); current gallbladder disease. Diabetes mellitus diagnosed >20 years ago may be UKMEC 3 or 4 depending on severity.

title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – UKMEC contraindications: UKMEC 4 conditions
content: UKMEC 4 conditions for the COCP (unacceptable health risk): age >35 years and smoking ≥15 cigarettes/day; migraine with aura; history of thromboembolic disease or thrombogenic mutation; history of stroke or ischaemic heart disease; breastfeeding <6 weeks post-partum; uncontrolled hypertension; current breast cancer; major surgery with prolonged immobilisation; positive antiphospholipid antibodies (e.g. in SLE).

title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Counselling: starting and taking the pill
content: If the COCP is started within the first 5 days of the cycle, no additional contraception is needed. If started at any other point, use alternative contraception (e.g. condoms) for the first 7 days. The pill should be taken at the same time every day. The conventional 21-day active pill followed by 7-day break is now supplemented by 'tailored' regimes (2019 guidelines): no pill-free interval, or 'tricycling' (three 21-day packs back-to-back before a 4–7 day break). There is no medical benefit from having a withdrawal bleed.

title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Counselling: factors reducing efficacy
content: Factors that may reduce COCP efficacy: vomiting within 2 hours of taking the pill; medications that induce diarrhoea or vomiting (e.g. orlistat); liver enzyme-inducing drugs. Concurrent non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics no longer require additional precautions (FSRH 2011 guidelines; BNF updated accordingly). Precautions should still be taken with enzyme-inducing antibiotics such as rifampicin.

title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Missed pill: 1 pill missed
content: FSRH guidance for COCP containing 30–35 micrograms ethinylestradiol: if 1 pill is missed at any time in the cycle, take the last pill even if it means taking two pills in one day, then continue taking pills daily. No additional contraceptive protection is needed.

title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Missed pill: 2 or more pills missed
content: If 2 or more COCP pills are missed: take the last pill even if it means taking two in one day, leave any earlier missed pills, and continue taking pills daily. Use condoms or abstain from sex until 7 consecutive days of pill-taking are re-established. If pills are missed in week 1 (Days 1–7): consider emergency contraception if unprotected sex occurred in the pill-free interval or in week 1. If missed in week 2 (Days 8–14): no emergency contraception needed after 7 consecutive days. If missed in week 3 (Days 15–21): finish the current pack and start a new pack the next day, omitting the pill-free interval.

title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Special situations: switching pills
content: When switching between COCP preparations, the BNF and FSRH give apparently contradictory advice. The FSRH Clinical Effectiveness Unit states the pill-free interval does not need to be omitted. The BNF advises missing the pill-free interval if the progestogen component changes. Given the uncertainty, it is best to follow the BNF guidance.

title: Contraception for women aged over 40 years – General principles
content: No method of contraception is contraindicated by age alone. All methods are UKMEC 1 for women over 40, except the COCP (UKMEC 2 for women ≥40 years) and Depo-Provera (UKMEC 2 for women >45 years). Women still require effective contraception until the menopause despite significantly declined fertility by age 40.

title: Contraception for women aged over 40 years – COCP and Depo-Provera considerations
content: COCP in perimenopausal women: may help maintain bone mineral density; may reduce menopausal symptoms; a pill containing <30 µg ethinylestradiol may be more suitable for women >40 years. Depo-Provera: women should be advised of a potential delay in return of fertility of up to 1 year for women >40 years; associated with a small loss in bone mineral density, usually recovered after discontinuation.

title: Contraception for women aged over 40 years – When to stop contraception
content: FSRH guidance on stopping contraception: Non-hormonal methods (IUD, condoms, natural family planning) – stop after 2 years of amenorrhoea if <50 years; after 1 year of amenorrhoea if ≥50 years. COCP – can be continued to age 50, then switch to non-hormonal or progestogen-only method. Implant, POP, IUS – can be continued beyond 50 years; if amenorrhoeic, check FSH and stop after 1 year if FSH ≥30 IU/L, or stop at 55 years.

title: Contraception for women aged over 40 years – HRT and contraception
content: HRT cannot be relied upon for contraception; a separate method is needed. The POP may be used with HRT as long as the HRT has a progestogen component (the POP cannot be relied upon to protect the endometrium). The IUS is licensed to provide the progestogen component of HRT.

title: Emergency contraception – Levonorgestrel: mechanism, dosing, and timing
content: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception: mode of action not fully understood; acts to stop ovulation and inhibit implantation. Single dose of levonorgestrel 1.5 mg (a progestogen). Must be taken within 72 hours of unprotected sexual intercourse (UPSI); efficacy decreases with time (84% effective if used within 72 hours). May be offered after 72 hours if the client is aware of reduced effectiveness (unlicensed indication). The dose should be doubled for BMI >26 or weight >70 kg, and for those taking enzyme-inducing drugs (although a copper IUD is preferable in the latter).

title: Emergency contraception – Levonorgestrel: safety and follow-up
content: Levonorgestrel is safe and well-tolerated. Disturbance of the current menstrual cycle is seen in a significant minority of women. Vomiting occurs in approximately 1%; if vomiting occurs within 3 hours the dose should be repeated. Levonorgestrel can be used more than once in a menstrual cycle if clinically indicated. Hormonal contraception can be started immediately after using levonorgestrel (Levonelle) for emergency contraception. Breastfeeding is not restricted after levonorgestrel use.

title: Emergency contraception – Ulipristal acetate: mechanism, dosing, and timing
content: Ulipristal acetate (EllaOne) is a selective progesterone receptor modulator. Primary mode of action is inhibition of ovulation.
