Dose: 30 mg orally as soon as possible, no later than 120 hours (5 days) after unprotected intercourse. Concomitant use with levonorgestrel is not recommended. Caution should be exercised in patients with severe asthma. Ulipristal can be used more than once in the same cycle.

title: Emergency contraception – Ulipristal acetate: effect on subsequent contraception and breastfeeding
content: Ulipristal may reduce the effectiveness of subsequent hormonal contraception. The pill, patch, or ring should be started or restarted 5 days after taking ulipristal; barrier methods should be used during this 5-day period. Breastfeeding should be delayed for one week after taking ulipristal. There are no such breastfeeding restrictions on levonorgestrel.

title: Emergency contraception – Copper IUD: efficacy and timing
content: The copper IUD is the most effective method of emergency contraception and should be offered to all women who meet the criteria. It is 99% effective regardless of where it is used in the cycle. Must be inserted within 5 days of UPSI; if a woman presents after more than 5 days, an IUD may be fitted up to 5 days after the likely ovulation date. The IUD may inhibit fertilisation or implantation. Prophylactic antibiotics may be given if the patient is at high risk of sexually transmitted infection.

title: Emergency contraception – Copper IUD: ongoing use and removal
content: The copper IUD used for emergency contraception may be left in situ to provide long-term contraception. If the client wishes for the IUD to be removed, it should be kept in place until at least the next period to ensure the emergency contraceptive effect is complete.

title: Epilepsy and contraception – UKMEC categories
content: For women taking phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, primidone, topiramate, or oxcarbazepine: COCP and POP are UKMEC 3; implant is UKMEC 2; Depo-Provera, IUD, and IUS are UKMEC 1. For lamotrigine: COCP is UKMEC 3; POP, implant, Depo-Provera, IUD, and IUS are UKMEC 1. If a COCP is chosen for women on lamotrigine, it should contain a minimum of 30 µg ethinylestradiol. The FSRH recommends consistent use of condoms in addition to other contraception for women with epilepsy.

title: Implantable contraceptives – Nexplanon: pharmacology and insertion
content: Nexplanon has replaced Implanon as the subdermal contraceptive implant. Both release the progestogen etonogestrel. Nexplanon improvements over Implanon: redesigned applicator to prevent deep insertions; radiopaque for easier localisation if impalpable. Inserted in the proximal non-dominant arm, just overlying the tricep. Primary mechanism: prevents ovulation; also thickens cervical mucus.

title: Implantable contraceptives – Nexplanon: efficacy, duration, and key advantages
content: Nexplanon is the most effective form of contraception (failure rate 0.07 per 100 woman-years). It lasts 3 years. It does not contain oestrogen and can therefore be used in women with a past history of thromboembolism or migraine. It can be inserted immediately following a termination of pregnancy. Additional contraceptive methods are needed for the first 7 days if not inserted on days 1–5 of the menstrual cycle.

title: Implantable contraceptives – Nexplanon: adverse effects and interactions
content: Main adverse effect: irregular or heavy bleeding (sometimes managed with co-prescription of COCP; speculum examination and STI check if bleeding continues). Progestogen effects: headache, nausea, breast pain. Interactions: enzyme-inducing drugs (certain antiepileptics and rifampicin) may reduce efficacy. FSRH advises switching to a method unaffected by enzyme-inducing drugs, or using additional contraception until 28 days after stopping the enzyme-inducing treatment.

title: Implantable contraceptives – Nexplanon: contraindications
content: UKMEC 3 contraindications for Nexplanon (proven risks generally outweigh advantages): ischaemic heart disease or stroke (for continuation; initiation is UKMEC 2); unexplained or suspicious vaginal bleeding; past breast cancer; severe liver cirrhosis; liver cancer. UKMEC 4 contraindication (unacceptable risk): current breast cancer.

title: Injectable contraceptives – Depo-Provera: pharmacology and dosing
content: Depo-Provera is the main injectable contraceptive used in the UK, containing medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg given via intramuscular injection every 12 weeks. It can be given up to 14 weeks after the last dose without the need for extra precautions (the BNF advises a pregnancy test if the interval is >12 weeks and 5 days, though this is not commonly adhered to in family planning). Primary mechanism: inhibits ovulation. Secondary effects: cervical mucus thickening and endometrial thinning.

title: Injectable contraceptives – Depo-Provera: adverse effects and contraindications
content: Adverse effects: irregular bleeding; weight gain; potential increased risk of osteoporosis (should only be used in adolescents if no other method is suitable); the injection cannot be reversed once given; delayed return to fertility (up to 12 months). Contraindications: current breast cancer is UKMEC 4; past breast cancer is UKMEC 3. Noristerat is the other injectable contraceptive licensed in the UK (given every 8 weeks), but is rarely used in clinical practice.

title: Intrauterine contraceptive devices – IUD vs IUS: mode of action and effectiveness
content: Both the IUD (copper) and IUS (levonorgestrel-releasing) are more than 99% effective. IUD mode of action: primary mechanism is prevention of fertilisation by decreasing sperm motility and survival, possibly via copper ions. IUS mode of action: levonorgestrel prevents endometrial proliferation and causes cervical mucus thickening. The IUS (Mirena) is also used in the management of menorrhagia.

title: Intrauterine contraceptive devices – IUD: duration and reliability
content: The copper IUD can be relied upon immediately following insertion. IUDs with copper on the stem only are effective for 5 years; IUDs with copper on both the stem and arms of the T may be effective for up to 10 years. IUDs make periods heavier, longer, and more painful.

title: Intrauterine contraceptive devices – IUS (Mirena): duration and bleeding effects
content: The Mirena IUS (levonorgestrel 20 mcg/24 hrs) can be relied upon after 7 days. It is effective for 8 years; if used in women ≥45 years, it is effective until age 55 years. If used as endometrial protection for women taking oestrogen-only HRT, it is only licensed for 5 years. Initially causes frequent uterine bleeding and spotting; later, women typically have intermittent light menses with less dysmenorrhoea, and some become amenorrhoeic.

title: Intrauterine contraceptive devices – Potential problems
content: Potential problems with IUDs/IUS: uterine perforation (up to 2 per 1,000 insertions; higher in breastfeeding women); ectopic pregnancy risk is increased proportionally but the absolute number of ectopics is reduced compared to no contraception; pelvic inflammatory disease (small increased risk in the first 20 days after insertion, returning to baseline thereafter); expulsion (risk approximately 1 in 20, most likely in the first 3 months).

title: Intrauterine contraceptive devices – Newer IUS systems: Jaydess and Kyleena
content: Jaydess IUS: licensed for 3 years; smaller frame and narrower inserter tube than Mirena; contains 13.5 mg levonorgestrel (compared to 52 mg in Mirena), resulting in lower serum LNG levels. Kyleena IUS: contains 19.5 mg LNG; smaller than Mirena; licensed for 5 years; lower serum LNG levels than Mirena; lower rate of amenorrhoea compared to Mirena.

title: Natural family planning – Clinical indicators of fertility
content: The major clinical indicators of fertility used in natural family planning are: changes in cervical mucus (becoming clearer, more slippery, and stretchy around ovulation); changes in the cervix (softer, higher, and more open around ovulation); and changes in basal body temperature (rises by approximately 0.2°C after ovulation).

title: Postpartum contraception – POP and COCP timing
content: After giving birth, women require contraception after day 21. POP: can be started at any time postpartum (breastfeeding and non-breastfeeding); after day 21, additional contraception should be used for the first 2 days; a small amount of progestogen enters breast milk but is not harmful to the infant. COCP: absolutely contraindicated (UKMEC 4) if breastfeeding <6 weeks post-partum; UKMEC 2 if breastfeeding 6 weeks–6 months; may reduce breast milk production; should not be used in the first 21 days due to increased VTE risk; after day 21, additional contraception for the first 7 days.

title: Postpartum contraception – IUD/IUS timing and lactational amenorrhoea method
content: The IUD or IUS can be inserted within 48 hours of childbirth or after 4 weeks (not between 48 hours and 4 weeks due to increased risk of expulsion). Lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM): 98% effective providing the woman is fully breastfeeding (no supplementary feeds), amenorrhoeic, and less than 6 months post-partum. An inter-pregnancy interval of less than 12 months between childbirth and conceiving again is associated with increased risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, and small for gestational age babies.

title: Progestogen-only pill – UKMEC 3 contraindications
content: UKMEC 3 conditions for the POP (disadvantages generally outweigh advantages): severe or decompensated liver cirrhosis; history of benign or malignant liver tumours; use of liver enzyme-inducing drugs (e.g. rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin); history of breast cancer more than 5 years ago; undiagnosed vaginal bleeding; ischaemic heart disease or stroke (for continuation); SLE with antiphospholipid antibodies; severe hypertension (systolic ≥160 mmHg or diastolic ≥100 mmHg); multiple cardiovascular risk factors.

title: Progestogen-only pill – UKMEC 4 contraindications
content: UKMEC 4 conditions for the POP (unacceptable health risk): current breast cancer (diagnosed within the last 5 years or ongoing disease); pregnancy (although not harmful if taken inadvertently during early pregnancy, the POP should not be initiated in pregnant individuals).

title: Progestogen-only pill – Counselling: starting and taking the POP
content: Most common problem: irregular vaginal bleeding. Starting: if commenced up to and including day 5 of the cycle, provides immediate protection; otherwise use additional contraception (e.g. condoms) for the first 2 days. If switching from a COCP, gives immediate protection if continued directly from the end of a pill packet (Day 21). The POP should be taken at the same time every day, without a pill-free break. Antibiotics have no effect on the POP (unless they alter the P450 enzyme system, e.g. rifampicin). Liver enzyme inducers may reduce effectiveness.

title: Progestogen-only pill – Missed pill rules: traditional POP vs Cerazette
content: Traditional POPs (Micronor, Noriday, Nogeston, Femulen): if less than 3 hours late, no action required; if more than 3 hours late (>27 hours since last pill), action needed. Cerazette (desogestrel): if less than 12 hours late, no action required; if more than 12 hours late (>36 hours since last pill), action needed. Action required: take the missed pill as soon as possible (one pill only even if multiple missed); continue rest of pack; use extra precautions (condoms) until pill-taking re-established for 48 hours.

title: Progestogen-only pill – Types: second and third generation
content: Second generation POPs: norethisterone, levonorgestrel, ethynodiol diacetate. Third generation POP: desogestrel (Cerazette). Cerazette differs from traditional POPs in that it inhibits ovulation in the majority of women (traditional POPs do not reliably inhibit ovulation) and allows a 12-hour window for missed pills (rather than 3 hours for traditional POPs).

title: Quick starting contraception – When pregnancy can be excluded
content: Quick starting (starting contraception outside the recommended time in the menstrual cycle) may require additional contraceptive precautions depending on the method and day of cycle: COCP (not Zoely or Qlaira) from day 6 onwards requires 7 days of additional contraception; POP (traditional/desogestrel) from day 6 onwards requires 2 days; progestogen-only injectable and implant from day 6 onwards require 7 days; LNG-IUS from day 8 onwards requires 7 days; copper IUD on any start day requires 0 additional days.

title: Quick starting contraception – When pregnancy cannot be excluded
content: If pregnancy cannot be excluded (negative pregnancy test but at risk from recent UPSI): assess and offer emergency contraception first. If levonorgestrel EC given: COCP, POP, or implant can commence immediately. If ulipristal EC given: delay quick-starting progestogen-containing contraception for 5 days (ulipristal effectiveness may be reduced by progestogen). Intrauterine contraception should not be offered unless pregnancy is reasonably excluded. A pregnancy test must be taken 21 days after the last UPSI.

title: Contraception for transgender and non-binary people – General principles
content: Contraceptive choices and sexual health guidance applies to any individual engaging in vaginal sex where there is a risk of pregnancy and/or STIs, regardless of gender identity. Sensitive communication and personalised options are essential. Condoms and dental dams are recommended for STI prevention. Cervical screening should be offered to all sexually active individuals with a uterus. HPV vaccination should be offered to all sexually active individuals.

title: Contraception for transgender and non-binary people – Contraceptive choices for trans men
content: For patients assigned female at birth with a uterus: testosterone therapy does not provide protection against pregnancy; if pregnancy occurs, testosterone is contraindicated (teratogenic). Oestrogen-containing regimes are not recommended during testosterone therapy (antagonise testosterone effects). Progestogen-only contraceptives are not considered to have a detrimental effect on testosterone therapy; IUS and injections may also suspend menstruation. Non-hormonal IUDs do not interact with hormonal regimes but may exacerbate menstrual bleeding. Either oral emergency contraceptive option may be used as neither is believed to interact with testosterone therapy.

title: Contraception for young people – Legal and ethical framework
content: The age of consent for sexual activity in the UK is 16 years. Practitioners may provide contraception to those under 16 if the young person is assessed as 'competent' using the Fraser Guidelines. Children under 13 cannot consent to sexual intercourse; consultations involving this age group must automatically trigger child protection measures. Fraser Guidelines require all of the following: the young person understands the advice; cannot be persuaded to inform parents; is likely to have sex with or without treatment; their health would suffer without treatment; and their best interests require receiving contraception.

title: Contraception for young people – Choice of method
content: Long-acting reversible contraceptive methods (LARCs) have advantages in young people due to less reliance on daily adherence. Concerns about Depo-Provera in young people: potential effect on bone mineral density. The UKMEC category for the IUS and IUD is 2 for women under 20 years, meaning they may not be the best choice. The progestogen-only implant (Nexplanon) is therefore the LARC of choice in young people. Young people should be advised to have STI tests 2 and 12 weeks after an incident of unprotected sexual intercourse.
